﻿# dsh-plugin-adoption

Rank DSH plugins by **real monthly npm downloads** instead of GitHub stars.
It carries two further i

ndependent dimensions: **capability-surface risk
(C0鈥揅3)** and **version line (will it even install?

endent dimensions: **capability-surface risk
(C0鈥揅3)** and **version line (will it even install?)**.
> 涓枃璇存槑瑙?README.zh.md銆?
## What it does and does not do

This plugin **reads** public sources and **ranks** what it finds. It does
not write, install, modify
or rate-limit anything.
| Reads | the 1024Store catalog API (public, read-only), npm's official downloads endpoint (public,

read-only), and the dsh-xray capability snapshot (public, read-only) |
| Writes | nothing 鈥?no file,

no config, no registry state, no other plugin |
| Network | GET only, to the public APIs, the npm r

egistry and dsh-xray |
| Registers | one tool, `plugin_adoption`. No HTTP route of its own |
| Modif
ies other plugins | never. It reports a ranking; it does not enforce one |

The two numbers it compares measure different things and the report says so
every time: **stars** me

asure the attention a repository received,
**downloads** measure installs that actually happened. Ne

ither is a quality
score, and this plugin does not produce one 鈥?it reports the disagreement
between
the two orderings and leaves the judgement to the caller.

Two things it deliberately does not do: it does not count plugins without an
npm package as zero (th

ey are listed separately, under `noPackage`), and it
does not hide a failed request behind an empty

result (they appear in
`requestFailures`, with the count of candidates that were actually compared).

The same rule governs the capability dimension: an ungraded plugin is reported
as `unknown`, never

e rule governs the capability dimension: an ungraded plugin is reported
as `unknown`, never as `C0`.

The catalog API allows 50 anonymous requests a day, so a default run samples
a bounded number of can
didates rather than the whole catalog.
## Why this exists

Community discovery surfaces order by **GitHub stars**. But a star measures the
attention a reposito

ry got, not an install that happened. Measured against the
live catalog on 2026-10-25:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
`dsh-mcp-panel` is **6th by stars (89) but 4th by downloads (10,058/month)** 鈥?an 89-star plugin tha
t more people actually run than a 240-star one.

**Stars can mislead; downloads don't.** This plugin puts both orderings side by
side and flags what
star ordering under-rates.
## Second dimension: capability-surface risk

Stars and downloads both answer "how many people use this". Neither answers
**"what can it do once i

nstalled on my machine"**.
dsh-xray publishes that by scanning each
plugin repository, and this plug
in joins it onto the candidate pool.
| Level | Meaning (quoted from the dsh-xray legend) |

| C0 | No notable capability surface. |
| C1 | Ordinary: registers tools/services, calls external do

mains. |
| C2 | Powerful: prompt surface, API interception, subprocess, exec, credential reads or in

stall scripts. |
| C3 | Powerful capabilities combined with sensitive behavior. |

This supplies a dimension neither the store nor the catalog has: of the store's
6,896 plugins only 6

24 have a download number, and none carries capability
data, while dsh-xray knows the capabilities b
ut not who installs them.
The report therefore gains two views:

- `topByRisk` 鈥?ordered by capability risk, worst first (ties broken by downloads)
- `highAdoptionAn

dHighRisk` 鈥?plugins that are **both widely installed and
sensitive**. This is the genuinely useful

line: which widely-installed plugins
can do sensitive things. The threshold is not invented: it is *

*half the
median download count of the candidate pool**, and the number used is
reported alongside s
o a reader can re-judge where the line should sit.

The governing rule: **ungraded is not safe**. A plugin with `level: null` lands
in the `unknown` buc

ket and is never sorted onto the "harmless" side 鈥?the same
principle as "no npm package is not zero

ever sorted onto the "harmless" side 鈥?the same
principle as "no npm package is not zero downloads".
In dsh-xray, `level: -1` is a **skipped** sentinel (measured: 349 records 鈥?324 `skipped: no scannab

le code`, 23 `skipped: download failed`, 2 scanner
errors). Those were never graded, so they are als

o `unknown`, and the original
`status` is preserved in `ungradedReason`.
## Limitations

- **Plugins without an npm package cannot be compared**; they are listed under
`noPackage` 鈥?"not pu

blished" and "nobody downloaded it" are different facts.
- Stars come from a catalog snapshot; downl

oads are npm's current-month window.
The two time windows differ.
- Downloads include CI, mirrors, a

nd automated installs 鈥?not purely "humans using it".
- Sampling depends on `queries`; it is not the

full catalog.
- **The capability grade is third-party static analysis, not a security rating.**
It

answers "what can this plugin do", not "is it malicious". C0 is not proof
of harmlessness either 鈥?i

t only means no notable surface was detected, and
static scanning cannot see behaviour that only app

ears at run time.
- The sensitive-flag subset (`SENSITIVE_FLAGS`) and the risk ordering weights are

**this plugin's judgement**, not dsh-xray's; only the C0鈥揅3 grades are the
publisher's. The two are

labelled separately in the code so you can disagree
with one without discarding the other.
- The bad

ge fallback yields **level only, no flags**, so `sensitive` is always
empty on that path 鈥?empty mea

ns "not fetched this time", not "no sensitive
capabilities".
- **The version line decides whether np

m would refuse the install, not whether
the plugin then runs.** A satisfied range is necessary, not

sufficient: a
wrong peer declaration or a changed runtime API can still install and break.
- The ver

sion line reads the `latest` version's peer block (that is what gets
installed). Historical versions

declare different ranges; this report does not
expand them one by one.
- At most 24 candidates are

checked per run; the rest are `unknown`, **not
"installs fine"**.
